title: What Does ABM Industries Actually Do? A Century of Sweeping Floors to Powering Microgrids

epigraph.quote: With $4.50 for a bucket, a mop, a sponge, a broom, and a brush, Morris Rosenberg did not just wash San Francisco's windows—he invented an industry out of outsourced operational reliability.
epigraph.author: Corporate History Archive

web_blocks.html: ABM Industries Incorporated (NYSE: ABM) is one of North America's largest integrated facility solutions providers [1]. The company employs roughly 113,000 people to clean, engineer, power, and maintain mission-critical client infrastructure [1, 2]. Its service footprint covers commercial buildings, airports, manufacturing plants, schools, and enterprise data centers [1, 2]. For fiscal year 2025, ABM generated $8,745.9 million in revenue (+4.6% year-over-year) and $162.4 million in GAAP net income [1, 3]. Trailing-twelve-month sales expanded further to reach $9.15 billion through Q3 FY2026 [4]. A fundamental structural tension defines this $9 billion enterprise top line. ABM remains a century-old, unionized janitorial operator with thin contract margins. Simultaneously, management acts as an acquisitive contractor pushing into semiconductor cleanrooms, airport infrastructure, and turnkey microgrids.

The company's origin story explains its operating DNA [5]. In 1909, German immigrant Morris Rosenberg lost his San Francisco hotel and restaurant business during an economic downturn [5]. Armed with $4.50, he bought a bucket, sponge, mop, broom, and brush [5, 6]. He went door-to-door offering to wash merchant shop windows for whatever owners thought the work was worth [5]. He cleared a $3.50 profit on day one [5, 6]. The firm incorporated as American Building Maintenance in 1913 and adopted the name ABM Industries in 1985 [5, 7]. For more than a century, the business proved a simple economic thesis [5]. Property owners prefer outsourcing hourly facility labor and collective bargaining administration [7]. They also avoid direct exposure to workers' compensation claims and round-the-clock maintenance schedules [5, 7].

web_blocks.html: Today, ABM reports across five primary operating segments [1]. Business & Industry (B&I) generates 47.2% of FY2025 revenue ($4,126.0 million) [1]. Manufacturing & Distribution (M&D) contributes 18.5% ($1,618.6 million) [1]. Aviation represents 12.8% ($1,118.7 million), while Technical Solutions (ATS) accounts for 11.0% ($960.6 million) [1]. Education delivers the remaining 10.5% ($922.0 million) [1]. B&I remains the largest profit contributor, generating $316.9 million in FY2025 segment operating profit [1]. However, post-pandemic hybrid work patterns and office vacancies continue to constrain top-line growth [1, 13]. Management counters this structural drag by prioritizing Class A trophy office towers and sports venues [13]. The firm also redirects capital into higher-margin specialized technical verticals.

Operating momentum through the first three quarters of FY2026 reveals both the upside and variability of this portfolio mix. In Q1 FY2026 (ended January 31, 2026), consolidated revenue rose 6.1% year-over-year to $2.2 billion [14]. Organic growth contributed 5.5%, propelled by double-digit expansion in Aviation and solid demand in Education [14]. In Q2 FY2026 (ended April 30, 2026), Technical Solutions surged 27% while Aviation expanded 20% year-over-year [15]. This quarter marked ABM's strongest consolidated organic revenue growth since Q3 2022 [15]. By Q3 FY2026 (ended July 31, 2026), quarterly revenue achieved a record $2.3 billion, rising +4.2% YoY [4, 16]. Organic revenue advanced 2.1%, while the WGNSTAR acquisition added another 2.1% [4, 16]. GAAP net income climbed 19% YoY to $49.7 million, reaching $0.84 per diluted share [4]. Aviation revenue expanded 12.5% to $328.1 million, supported by the London Heathrow contract ramp-up [4, 16]. Concurrently, ATS growth cooled to 4.2% ($259.9 million) as enterprise clients deferred project starts [4, 16].

This quarterly cadence demonstrates why investors cannot evaluate ABM as a simple uniform compounder. Legacy janitorial and school contracts supply a steady, recurring cash baseline [4, 10]. In contrast, technical verticals introduce project milestone timing and working-capital swings [11, 12]. These activities include microgrid EPC installations, data-center UPS commissioning, and semiconductor tool maintenance [10, 11, 12]. Understanding how these two distinct operating rhythms coexist forms the core foundation of our audit.

web_blocks.title: THE CORE IDENTITY: LABOR AGGREGATOR MEETS INFRASTRUCTURE CONTRACTOR
paragraphs: ABM is not a software enterprise or a capital-light franchise. It operates as a labor-intensive contractor with 113,000 employees deployed across client sites daily [2]. Its economic moat stems from national scale and experienced union labor administration [7]. The firm also provides rigorous multi-site regulatory compliance [7]. Increasingly, ABM leverages specialized technical credentials across microgrids, UPS power architectures, and semiconductor cleanrooms [10, 11, 12].

book_paragraphs: Every great industrial story starts with a problem nobody else wanted to solve. In 1909, Morris Rosenberg stood on a dusty San Francisco street with $4.50 in his pocket, a bucket, a mop, a sponge, a broom, and a brush. His hotel and restaurant business had just failed, and the city's shopkeepers were staring at grime-streaked storefront windows. Rosenberg offered to clean them for whatever the merchants thought the job was worth. By dusk, he had his $4.50 back plus $3.50 in profit. More importantly, he had discovered a truth that still powers ABM Industries more than a century later: businesses will gladly pay someone else to handle the messy, labor-intensive, unglamorous work required to keep physical spaces running.

If you walk into a Class A Manhattan office tower, a bustling international terminal at London Heathrow or Los Angeles International Airport, an automated e-commerce warehouse, a public school district, or a semiconductor fabrication plant today, there is a remarkably high chance that an ABM Industries uniform is somewhere in the building. With roughly 113,000 employees and $8.75 billion in fiscal 2025 revenue—crossing $9.15 billion on a trailing-twelve-month basis in 2026—ABM is one of the largest facility solutions enterprises in North America.

Yet if you stop at 'janitorial company,' you will completely misunderstand what ABM is trying to become. Over the past decade, CEO Scott Salmirs and his leadership team have waged a relentless, capital-intensive campaign to move ABM up the technical value chain. You and I need to see this clearly from the outset: ABM is a business with two distinct souls living under one corporate roof.

The first soul is the legacy recurring-services engine. This is the world of multi-year janitorial, parking, shuttle, and stationary building engineering contracts across Business & Industry (47.2% of FY2025 revenue), Education (10.5%), and Aviation (12.8%). It is sticky, essential, and recession-resistant—trash still has to be emptied, airport shuttles still have to run, and classrooms still have to be sanitized. But it is also a low-margin, wage-sensitive grind where a single mispriced union contract or a wave of commercial office vacancies can compress profitability.

The second soul is the technical infrastructure and mission-critical solutions engine—anchored by Technical Solutions (11.0% of FY2025 revenue) and the high-tech side of Manufacturing & Distribution (18.5%). Since 2017, ABM has spent over $2.6 billion buying its way into higher-margin, harder-to-replicate capabilities. It bought GCA Services Group for ~$1.25 billion in 2017 to dominate K-12 and university facilities. It paid $830 million in cash for Able Services in 2021 to become an engineering powerhouse. It acquired RavenVolt in 2022 for $170 million upfront (plus earn-outs) to build turnkey commercial microgrids. In June 2024, it spent roughly $118 million for Quality Uptime Services to maintain uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) for data centers. And in February 2026, it closed a $275 million all-cash deal for WGNSTAR, pushing its specialized semiconductor fab portfolio to roughly $325 million in annualized revenue.

Through the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, you can see that dual-engine structure in motion. Revenue hit a record $2.3 billion in Q3 FY2026, propelled by a 12.5% surge in Aviation and steady M&D demand, even as Technical Solutions navigated client project deferrals after a 27% jump in Q2. Meanwhile, ABM has raised its dividend for 58 consecutive years—earning a rare seat among Dividend Kings. The central question we will audit across the next five chapters is whether ABM's high-tech acquisitions and digital 'ELEVATE' transformation are truly changing the company's underlying economics, or whether the gravitational pull of 113,000 hourly workers and $2.59 billion in goodwill keeps returns anchored to earth.

book_subsections.title: A Century of Consolidation: From Window Washing to Cleanrooms
paragraphs: When you trace ABM's timeline from 1909 to 2026, you see a textbook roll-up playbook. In its early decades, American Building Maintenance expanded up and down the West Coast by offering standardized cleaning and lighting maintenance. By the 1960s and 1970s, it had gone public (IPO in 1969) and broadened into parking, security, and mechanical engineering. Each decade brought new acronyms and bolt-on acquisitions, culminating in the modern five-segment architecture.

What changed after 2017 was the scale and technical ambition of the deals. GCA Services Group doubled down on institutional education and manufacturing. Able Services neutralized ABM's largest private rival in stationary engineering—the licensed technicians who keep chillers, boilers, and HVAC systems running in skyscrapers. Then came RavenVolt, Quality Uptime, and WGNSTAR: three bets on electrification, AI data center uptime, and domestic semiconductor manufacturing. Instead of merely cleaning buildings, ABM now designs backup power microgrids and manages cleanroom tools inside chip fabs.

Yet every bolt-on acquisition leaves a permanent imprint on the balance sheet and culture. Integrating 113,000 employees across legacy janitorial crews, unionized airport shuttle drivers, and elite cleanroom engineers is no small feat. As we trace ABM's evolution, remember that revenue scale is easy to buy with cash and debt; operational integration and higher returns on capital are much harder to earn.

book_subsections.title: What a Century of Cycles Teaches Us About ABM's DNA
paragraphs: If you step back and look at ABM's journey from Morris Rosenberg's $4.50 bucket-and-ladder operation in 1909 San Francisco to a $9.15 billion enterprise, one pattern jumps off the page: ABM has always survived and grown by trading up the complexity ladder whenever legacy cleaning commoditized. In the 1950s and 1960s, it moved from simple window washing into full-building engineering and parking management. In the 2000s and 2010s, it consolidated regional rivals like GCA Services Group and Able Services to build national scale.

Yet every major acquisition wave also left the same scar on the balance sheet: higher leverage and a larger pile of goodwill that took years of steady cash flow to digest. When ABM bought Able Services for $830 million in 2021 right as commercial offices were emptying out for remote work, the market punished the stock until management proved it could pivot toward aviation, manufacturing, and RavenVolt microgrids. That century-long rhythm tells you everything about ABM's DNA: it is a resilient, cash-generative operator that periodically overpays for scale and then spends three to five years repairing its balance sheet.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When a 117-year-old janitorial giant starts talking about microgrids and semiconductor cleanrooms, your first instinct as an analyst should be healthy skepticism. Acquisitions can buy revenue growth overnight, but they also pile up goodwill, debt, and integration complexity. Before we celebrate the transformation, we have to examine every single segment on the ground—customer by customer, contract by contract.
